definition: Building optical components (modulators, waveguides, detectors) on silicon wafers with chip-making tools, so light-based links can be made in volume and placed next to electronic chips.

The digital signal processor inside a pluggable transceiver that cleans up and retimes the high-speed signal. Supplied mainly by Marvell and Broadcom; removing it (linear optics) saves power at the cost of reach.

A copper cable with retimer chips in its connectors that extend reach to several metres at 100-200G per lane, cheaper and lower-power than optics for in-rack and adjacent-rack links. Credo is the leading supplier.
A switch that steers light beams with tiny mirrors to reconnect fibers without converting to electrical signals. Google uses OCS in place of spine switches in Jupiter and in TPU pods.

A switch chip with large packet memory (often HBM), such as Broadcom Jericho or Cisco P200, that can absorb bursts over long links. Used for scale-across between data centers and for scheduled AI fabrics.
A switch built by an ODM (e.g. Celestica, Accton) on merchant silicon, sold without a vendor operating system; the buyer runs SONiC, FBOSS or its own software.
The software that runs a switch: routing, telemetry, configuration. Examples are Arista EOS, Cisco NX-OS, NVIDIA Cumulus Linux and the open-source SONiC.
How much of one product a customer buys alongside another, e.g. dollars of networking per dollar of GPUs. A rising attach rate means a vendor captures more of each cluster's budget.
Wall-clock time to finish a training job or step. Network vendors quote JCT gains because they capture both bandwidth and tail-latency effects.
